title: The Water Cycle
description: How water moves continuously through Earth's atmosphere, surface, and subsurface

concepts.title: The Hydrological Cycle
concepts.contentHtml:
Water is continuously recycled between the ocean, atmosphere, land, and subsurface in the hydrological (water) cycle. Key processes:

  • Evaporation — solar energy drives water from ocean and land surface into the atmosphere as vapour. ~90 % of atmospheric water comes from ocean evaporation.
  • Transpiration — plants release water vapour through leaf pores. Together with evaporation this is called evapotranspiration.
  • Condensation — water vapour cools and forms clouds (liquid droplets or ice crystals).
  • Precipitation — water returns to the surface as rain, snow, sleet, or hail.
  • Runoff and infiltration — water flows over the surface (runoff) or sinks into the ground (infiltration).

concepts.title: Global Water Distribution
concepts.contentHtml:
Earth has approximately 1.386 billion km³ of water. Its distribution:

  • 96.5 % — oceans (salt water)
  • 1.7 % — groundwater (mostly fresh)
  • 1.7 % — ice sheets and glaciers
  • 0.01 % — rivers and lakes
  • 0.001 % — atmosphere

Although rivers and lakes seem abundant on the surface, they contain a tiny fraction of total water. The enormous majority is locked in oceans and ice — making freshwater an inherently limited resource.

concepts.title: Residence Times
concepts.contentHtml:
The time water spends in each reservoir — its residence time — varies enormously:

  • Atmosphere: ~9 days
  • Rivers: ~2–6 months
  • Soil moisture: 1–2 months
  • Groundwater: hundreds to thousands of years
  • Ice sheets: up to ~100,000 years
  • Deep ocean: ~3,000 years

Residence times matter for water resource management. Groundwater pumped from deep aquifers may be water that fell as rain thousands of years ago — it is not being recharged on human timescales. Once depleted, it cannot be replaced in any practical sense.

title: Rivers and Fluvial Processes
description: How rivers carve landscapes and carry sediment to the sea

concepts.title: River Dynamics
concepts.contentHtml:
Rivers transport water and sediment downhill under gravity. Their behaviour is governed by the balance between erosion (picking up sediment), transport, and deposition:

  • Fast-moving water in steep, narrow channels erodes and transports large particles.
  • Slow-moving water in flat, wide floodplains deposits fine sediment.

A river's ability to transport sediment is proportional to roughly the sixth power of its velocity — small speed increases dramatically increase carrying capacity. This is why floods, though brief, transport enormous volumes of sediment and reshape channels overnight.

concepts.title: Meanders and Oxbow Lakes
concepts.contentHtml:
On flat terrain, rivers develop meanders — sinuous S-curves. The outer bank of each curve is eroded by fast-moving water; the inner bank accumulates sediment as a point bar. The meander migrates and grows until the neck between two loops becomes narrow.

During a major flood, the river can cut across the neck, abandoning the old loop. The cut-off loop becomes an oxbow lake — a curved lake with no active river flow. The Mississippi River has hundreds of oxbow lakes along its floodplain, recording centuries of meander migration.

The Amazon River, at 6,400 km the world's largest by discharge (~20 % of global river runoff), displays spectacular meander systems across the Amazon Basin.

concepts.title: River Systems and Drainage Basins
concepts.contentHtml:
A drainage basin (catchment or watershed) is all the land that drains to a single outlet. Drainage basins are separated by topographic highs called divides.

The world's major river systems:
— Amazon (~7 million km² basin) — largest by discharge and basin area.
— Congo — largest by volume in Africa; deepest river in the world (~220 m).
— Nile (~6,650 km) — traditionally listed as the world's longest river; drains northeast Africa.
— Yangtze — China's longest river; its basin supports around 400 million people.
— Mississippi-Missouri — drains ~40 % of the continental USA.

title: Groundwater and Aquifers
description: The hidden ocean beneath our feet

concepts.title: How Groundwater Works
concepts.contentHtml:
When rain falls, some runs off the surface and some infiltrates the soil. Water that penetrates deep enough reaches the water table — the upper surface of the saturated zone where all pore spaces are filled with water.

Rock layers that store and transmit significant quantities of groundwater are called aquifers. The best aquifers have high porosity (space for water) and high permeability (interconnected pores allowing flow). Well-sorted sandstone and fractured limestone make excellent aquifers.

Confining layers (aquitards) of impermeable clay or shale can trap water under pressure, creating artesian aquifers where wells flow freely without pumping.

concepts.title: Major Aquifers and Groundwater Depletion
concepts.contentHtml:
Groundwater is the world's most important freshwater resource — providing drinking water for over 2 billion people. Key aquifers:

  • Ogallala (High Plains) Aquifer, USA — underlies ~450,000 km² of the US Great Plains; sustains ~30 % of US groundwater irrigation. Being depleted orders of magnitude faster than it recharges — some areas have dropped >100 m.
  • Great Artesian Basin, Australia — one of the world's largest artesian aquifers; recharges from rain on the Eastern Highlands over thousands of years.
  • Nubian Sandstone Aquifer, North Africa — 'fossil water' from Pleistocene rains, 40,000 years old; being pumped by Libya and Egypt.

concepts.title: Springs, Karst, and Sinkholes
concepts.contentHtml:
Where the water table intersects the land surface, groundwater emerges as a spring. Springs have been crucial to human settlement — many ancient cities were founded on reliable spring lines.

Karst topography develops where groundwater dissolves soluble bedrock (usually limestone or dolomite). Carbonic acid in rainwater reacts with calcium carbonate, slowly opening caves, disappearing streams, and sinkholes — circular collapse features that can swallow buildings overnight.

Famous karst regions include the Dinaric Alps of the former Yugoslavia (where 'karst' is named), the Yucatan Peninsula (Mexico), and Florida's sinkhole belt. The Yucatan cenotes (flooded sinkholes) were sacred to the Maya and connected to the Chicxulub crater's impact geology.

title: Glaciers and Ice Sheets
description: Frozen water as a geological agent — and as a climate record

concepts.title: How Glaciers Form and Move
concepts.contentHtml:
A glacier forms where snow accumulates faster than it melts year over year. Under pressure, snow recrystallises into ice. When ice is thick enough, it flows under its own weight — partly by internal crystal deformation and partly by sliding on a thin water film at its base.

Glaciers flow from the accumulation zone (where snow builds up) to the ablation zone (where melting or calving removes ice). A glacier in equilibrium has equal accumulation and ablation. As climate warms, ablation exceeds accumulation and the glacier retreats.

Valley glaciers scour U-shaped valleys; ice sheets can cover entire continents. At their maximum extent, Pleistocene ice sheets covered 30 % of Earth's land surface.

concepts.title: Glacial Erosion and Deposition
concepts.contentHtml:
Glaciers are among the most powerful erosional agents on Earth. They carve distinctive landforms:

  • Cirques — armchair-shaped hollows where glaciers originate.
  • Arêtes — sharp ridges between adjacent cirques.
  • Horns — pyramidal peaks where multiple cirques meet (e.g. the Matterhorn, Switzerland).
  • Fjords — drowned glacial valleys (e.g. Norway's Sognefjord, ~1,300 m deep).

Glacial deposition leaves behind moraines (ridges of unsorted debris), drumlins (streamlined mounds), and erratic boulders transported far from their origin. New York's Long Island is largely a terminal moraine from the last glaciation.

concepts.title: Ice Cores — Frozen Climate Archives
concepts.contentHtml:
Deep ice cores drilled from ice sheets preserve annual layers of snow, trapping air bubbles that contain samples of ancient atmosphere. The EPICA dome C core from Antarctica extends back 800,000 years — the most detailed climate record available for that period.

Ice cores reveal:
— Temperature history (from oxygen isotope ratios in ice).
— Past CO₂ and methane concentrations (from trapped air bubbles).
— Volcanic eruptions (sulfate layers).
— Dust storms, fires, and industrial pollution.

The Antarctic Ice Sheet holds ~70 % of Earth's fresh water. If it melted completely, global sea levels would rise ~58 m — enough to flood most coastal cities on Earth.

title: Water, Climate, and the Future
description: Changing cycles, sea-level rise, and the coming water crisis

concepts.title: Sea-Level Rise and Coastal Hydrology
concepts.contentHtml:
Global mean sea level has risen ~20 cm since 1900, with the rate accelerating. Two main contributions:
— Thermal expansion: warmer oceans take up more volume (~30 % of current rise).
— Ice melt: Greenland and Antarctic ice sheets, plus mountain glaciers (~70 %).

In coastal aquifers, sea-level rise drives saltwater intrusion — saltwater displaces freshwater in coastal aquifers, contaminating drinking water. Miami, Jakarta, and many Pacific island nations already face this problem. As low-lying coastal land sinks (subsidence from groundwater extraction) while sea levels rise, the twin pressures compound.

concepts.title: River Systems Under Climate Change
concepts.contentHtml:
Climate change alters river hydrology in several ways:
— Glacier-fed rivers (Indus, Ganges, Yellow River) initially receive more meltwater as glaciers retreat, then dramatically less when glaciers are gone — threatening water security for billions of people in Asia.
— Increased flood frequency — warmer air holds more moisture, intensifying precipitation events.
— Longer droughts — reduced river baseflow between rain events.

The Colorado River (USA) is severely over-allocated: seven US states and Mexico have legal rights to more water than the river carries in most years. Lake Mead, the river's largest reservoir, dropped to its lowest level ever in 2022.

concepts.title: The Global Water Crisis
concepts.contentHtml:
By 2050, over 5 billion people may face water scarcity for at least part of the year. Hydrologists identify several converging crises:

  • Groundwater overdraft — aquifers depleted faster than recharge rates across India, China, the Middle East, and the USA.
  • Shrinking lakes — the Aral Sea (Central Asia) was once the world's 4th largest lake; by 2007 it had lost ~90 % of its volume due to Soviet-era irrigation. Lake Chad (West Africa) has shrunk ~90 % since 1960.
  • Virtual water trade — countries import water-intensive crops rather than deplete domestic supplies, but this doesn't solve global scarcity.

Geology determines where water resources exist; hydrology determines how to manage them sustainably.
